young.html: A symposium was a dinner party in ancient Athens. In Plato's Symposium, a poet named Agathon has just won a prize for a play, and his friends come to celebrate. Instead of playing games, they decide that each guest will give a speech in praise of Love.

The speeches are all different. The comic poet Aristophanes tells a funny story: long ago, people were round, with four arms and four legs, and rolled along like wheels! The gods split them in two, and ever since, each of us has been looking for our other half.

Then Socrates speaks. He says he learned about love from a wise woman named Diotima. She taught him that love is wanting something beautiful and good. And she described a ladder: you start by loving one beautiful thing, then you notice beauty in many things, then in good character, in fair laws, in knowledge, and finally you see Beauty itself, the source of all the rest.

young.name: gb-diotima-ladder
young.cap: Climb Diotima's ladder, one step at a time.

young.html: A beauty ladder of your own. Draw a ladder with five steps. On the bottom step, write or draw one beautiful thing you love (a flower, a song, a pet). On the next, many beautiful things like it. Then something beautiful about a person's character, like kindness. Then a beautiful rule or custom, like taking turns. At the top, write what you think all of them share.

In another dialogue, the Phaedrus, Socrates compares the soul to a chariot pulled by two winged horses, one calm and noble and one wild, with a driver trying to steer them both. Most of us know that feeling!

full.html: The Symposium (about 385–370 BC) is set in 416 BC, at the house of the poet Agathon the day after his first win in the tragedy competition. The story is told years later by Apollodorus, who heard it from a guest. The guests agree to drink lightly and each give a speech in praise of Eros, the god of love.

head: Speaker
His speech, in brief
rows: Love is the oldest god, and lovers are the bravest people, because they would be ashamed to act badly in front of the one they love.
There are two loves, a heavenly one that cares for the other person's mind and character, and a common one that does not.
Love is a force of balance and harmony throughout nature, in medicine, music and the seasons.
Humans were once double, round creatures; Zeus split them, and love is the search for one's other half.
Love is the youngest, most beautiful and best of the gods.
Love is the desire for the beautiful and good, which we lack; he reports what Diotima taught him.
Arriving late and noisy, he praises Socrates himself instead.
full.cap: The speeches of the Symposium, in our own words.

full.html: Socrates first gets Agathon to admit that love wants beauty, so love cannot itself be beautiful, any more than a thirsty person is full. Diotima, he says, taught him that Love is not a god but a spirit between gods and mortals, always needy and always resourceful. What love really wants is to have the good for ever. Mortals reach for that by “giving birth in beauty”: children, poems, laws, and ideas that outlast us.

full.text: And the true order of going, or being led by another, to the things of love, is to begin from the beauties of earth and mount upwards for the sake of that other beauty, using these as steps only, and from one going on to two, and from two to all fair forms, and from fair forms to fair practices, and from fair practices to fair notions, until from fair notions he arrives at the notion of absolute beauty, and at last knows what the essence of beauty is.
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. I, Clarendon Press

full.name: gb-diotima-ladder
full.cap: The ladder, in our own words. Tap a step or climb with the buttons.

full.html: Beauty itself is one of Plato's Forms: the pattern that every beautiful thing shares in, which never grows, fades or depends on the viewer. “Platonic love,” in the later sense of a love that is not about the body, comes from readings of this passage.

Alcibiades, a brilliant and controversial Athenian general, arrives with a crowd and, instead of praising Love, praises Socrates. Socrates, he says, is like the little statues of Silenus sold in the market: ugly outside, but open them and there are images of gods inside. He tells how Socrates saved his life in battle, walked barefoot on ice, and once stood thinking in one spot for a day and a night. The party ends at dawn with Socrates still talking, and then going off to spend the day as usual.

full.text: The Phaedrus: the chariot of the soul

full.html: The Phaedrus (about 370 BC) takes place outside the city walls, by a stream under a plane tree, with the cicadas singing. Phaedrus has a speech by the orator Lysias; Socrates answers it with two speeches of his own. In the second he describes the soul:

full.text: And let the figure be composite—a pair of winged horses and a charioteer. Now the winged horses and the charioteers of the gods are all of them noble and of noble descent, but those of other races are mixed; the human charioteer drives his in a pair; and one of them is noble and of noble breed, and the other is ignoble and of ignoble breed; and the driving of them of necessity gives a great deal of trouble to him.
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. I, Clarendon Press

full.html: The charioteer is reason; the good horse is like the spirited part of us that cares about honor; the unruly horse is appetite. Seeing beauty, Socrates says, reminds the soul of the Forms it once saw, and makes its wings begin to grow again.

The second half of the Phaedrus asks what makes a speech good. A good speech, Socrates says, is put together like a living creature, with a head, a body and feet that fit; and a real speaker must know the truth and understand the souls of the listeners. Then he tells a story of the Egyptian god Theuth, who invented writing, and King Thamus, who warned that it would make people forgetful. Socrates adds:

full.text: I cannot help feeling, Phaedrus, that writing is unfortunately like painting; for the creations of the painter have the attitude of life, and yet if you ask them a question they preserve a solemn silence.
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. I, Clarendon Press

full.html: Missing the irony that Plato makes this point in writing. Many readers think that is why he wrote dialogues: conversations on the page that invite you to answer back.

deep.html: Readers have long noticed how much these dialogues ask of the reader. The speakers praise love in the customs of their own time and place, which were different from ours. Diotima then says that the lower rungs are only steps. Some readers think Plato makes the love of particular people only a means to something higher; others think the ladder keeps every rung, and that loving beauty itself makes us love people better. Aristotle's discussion of friendship, in the Ethics later on this ladder, puts loving another person for his own sake at the center.

deep.text: What later writers did with it

deep.html: Plotinus built much of his thought on Diotima's ascent, and through him it reached Augustine and the Middle Ages. Dante's journey toward the vision of God in the Paradiso is often compared to it. The Phaedrus's warning about writing is quoted today in debates about calculators, the internet and other aids to memory.

items: Is beauty in the thing or in the eye of the beholder? What would Diotima say?
Does loving one beautiful thing help you see beauty in others, or keep you from it?
Does writing things down help you remember, or make you forget? What about photos on a phone?

questions: Which speech at the party do you like best, and why?
Aristophanes says we are all looking for our “other half.” Is that a good picture of friendship? What might be missing?
What are the most beautiful things you know? What do they have in common?
Socrates compares the soul to a driver with two horses. When have you felt pulled in two directions? Who won?
Is a book like a painting that can't answer questions? How could a book answer back?
Is a kind person more beautiful than a handsome one? Why might Diotima say so?
care: The guests talk about love in the customs of ancient Athens, and Alcibiades arrives drunk. Nothing is described graphically. For young readers, focus on Aristophanes' story, Diotima's ladder of beauty and the Phaedrus's chariot.
